<jats:p>
                    <jats:boxed-text orientation="portrait" position="float">
                      <jats:p>
                        <jats:bold>Anterior Versus Posterior Insular Epilepsy: Correlations With Semiology Based on Stereoelectroencephalography</jats:bold>
                      </jats:p>
                      <jats:p>Chisholm J, Krishnan B, Khoury J, Alexopoulos A, Bingaman W, Serletis D, Najm I, Bulacio JC. Ann Neurol. 2025 Nov;98(5):1111-1124. doi: 10.1002/ana.70015. Epub 2025 Aug 13. PMID: 40799141; PMCID: PMC12577678.</jats:p>
                      <jats:p>
                        Objective: To characterize insular seizure semiology and correlate with stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) seizure onset in a well-defined cohort, in particular examining differences between anterior and posterior insular seizures. Methods: We documented all semiological signs and the timing of emergence for 45 patients with SEEG-confirmed insular epilepsy, along with the precise location of the seizure onset zone (SOZ) within the insula. Semiological signs and other noninvasive data were compared between those with anterior and posterior insula SOZ, with more detailed insular subregion description when appropriate. Co-occurrence patterns of insular semiological signs were also investigated. Results: A total of 87% reported auras, and the corresponding insular SOZ demonstrated an anterior-to-posterior gradient by aura type. The absence of aura was significantly associated with an anterior insula SOZ (
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                        = 0.01). Late grunting/moaning (
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                        = 0.07), symmetric mouth elementary motor (
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                        = 0.1), blinking (
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                        = 0.05), and chewing/repetitive swallowing (
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                        = 0.09) also suggested an anterior insula SOZ. Unilateral nonpainful somatosensory aura (
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                        = 0.07) and early arm/hand elementary motor (
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                        = 0.1) suggested a posterior insular SOZ. Interpretation: We report the characteristics and semiological features in a large cohort of primary insular epilepsy patients. The type of aura is crucial for identifying the SOZ, and the timing of semiological emergence contributes to the anatomo-electro-clinical localization of an insular SOZ. These findings can enhance the identification of insular epilepsy, making targeted curative treatment feasible.
                      </jats:p>
                    </jats:boxed-text>
                  </jats:p>
title: Avoiding Insularity: Insights in Insular Semiology From sEEG

items.abstract: <jats:p>Epilepsy represents a multifaceted group of disorders divided into two broad categories, partial and generalized, based on the seizure onset zone. The identification of the neuroanatomic site of seizure onset depends on delineation of seizure semiology by a careful history together with video-EEG, and a variety of neuroimaging technologies such as MRI, fMRI, FDG-PET, MEG, or invasive intracranial EEG recording. Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the commonest form of focal epilepsy and represents almost 2/3 of cases of intractable epilepsy managed surgically. A history of febrile seizures (especially complex febrile seizures) is common in TLE and is frequently associated with mesial temporal sclerosis (the commonest form of TLE). Seizure auras occur in many TLE patients and often exhibit features that are relatively specific for TLE but few are of lateralizing value. Automatisms, however, often have lateralizing significance. Careful study of seizure semiology remains invaluable in addressing the search for the seizure onset zone.</jats:p>
